stories.Headline: AI Hiring Push Might Change The Case For Investing In Disney (DIS)
stories.Summary:
Walt Disney has moved to license intellectual property from bankrupt chatbot startup Character.AI and plans to hire most of its roughly 60 person workforce. The company would pay about US$60 million in annual compensation for that hiring push. Disney also made a US$20 million bid for certain Character.AI assets. The aim is to bring conversational AI capabilities in house for use across streaming and park experiences.

The move ties into Disney's existing push on data and AI under its new Chief Technology Officer. Stronger internal AI capabilities could help customer engagement in parks, cruises and Disney+ and offer tools to manage support and content workflows more efficiently. The article describes the hiring move as incremental rather than transformational in the short run. It says the move does not materially change Disney's near term drivers, which include streaming profitability, softer ad markets and content spend.

The article says Character.AI's legal and regulatory overhangs highlight execution risk around AI, brand safety and potential litigation. It places that risk alongside streaming ad softness and regional park demand on the risk list. Analyst consensus cited in the article points to revenues of US$113.7b and earnings of US$13.5b by 2029. That assumes revenue expanding at about 4.8% a year and earnings rising by roughly US$4.9b from US$8.6b today.

The article also notes a long running royalty deal for Jason Weaver's young Simba role in The Lion King, which it says shows how Disney's intellectual property can keep generating inheritable payments for talent. Five fair value views from the Simply Wall St Community cluster between US$124.24 and US$134.63. The article says Disney's fair value indicates a 14% potential upside to its current price. It adds that the spread could narrow quickly.

Articles.Title: AI Hiring Push Might Change The Case For Investing In Disney (DIS)

stories.Headline: I built a programming language that LLMs can't use
stories.Summary:
A developer who writes at blog.picheta.me built a programming language called KillSwitch and published an account of it on October 17, 2026. The developer said the aim was to test whether large language models understand code or mainly recall snippets from training data and context windows. KillSwitch is described as an esoteric language designed to be adversarial to LLMs and coding agents while still usable by humans. The interpreter and language specification are open source and available on GitHub.

The language includes hidden lies in its spec that humans are unlikely to read or would recognize as lies, and it expects human readers to deduce certain things rather than having them explained. Counting letters in identifiers is crucial, and the interpreter refuses to run code that breaks rules based on character counts. Some constructs are designed to trigger model safety guardrails, and the phrase "Ignore previous instructions" has meaning in the language to confuse models. Scripts are mostly noise, made up mostly of stories that can embed syntactically relevant instructions but do not need to, and literals can be placed anywhere in a script and referenced using line counts. KillSwitch is fundamentally a stack-based interpreted language with a limited set of constructs including functions, variables and if statements.

The developer devised a set of tasks and benchmarked major LLM models and coding agent harnesses against them, with a chart and leaderboard at bench.killswitch-lang.org. Claude's Opus 5 performs best, not Opus 5.5, and the developer said the difference does not appear to be pure chance because Opus 5 is better at interpreting the spec. Some models, including Fable 5.1 and Gemini 4 Argon, do poorly because of overly sensitive safety guardrails, and the best open-weight model is MiMo-V2.6-Pro. The best performing model scores 66.8.

The developer argued that this does not prove LLMs can understand the code, because the benchmark tasks are fairly simple, including implementing hello world, explaining what a script that prints the max of two numbers will output, and modifying a script that converts celsius to fahrenheit to do the inverse conversion. The developer said it is impressive that models can solve these tasks for a novel language built to confuse them but that it is not a clear signal of understanding. The developer plans to watch how soon-to-be-released models handle the current tasks and, if they complete them all successfully, to devise another, more complex task set. The developer also said it is encouraging that model performance on this simple set of tasks correlates with other model benchmarks.

Articles.Title: I built a programming language that LLMs can't use

stories.Headline: AI and US-China rivalry put universities to the test: Vanderbilt head
stories.Summary:
Vanderbilt University Chancellor Daniel Diermeier spoke to Nikkei Asia about how universities are coping with the U.S.-China race for technology and AI dominance. He said schools must keep pace with rapid advances while managing growing security compliance requirements. The interview was published on October 18, 2026, and covered concerns about national security. Diermeier said universities must contend with real worries, particularly on high-risk technology and dual-use technology.

The demands on universities include staying relevant as AI develops quickly and meeting security rules that keep expanding. Diermeier described security compliance as an ever-growing requirement for schools. He said universities can endure the change despite the pressure. The article gives no specific figures, dates or policy names beyond the interview date.

Diermeier is responsible for leading Vanderbilt, based in Nashville, Tennessee, and he framed the challenge as one of balancing openness with security. He acknowledged genuine national security concerns around sensitive technologies. He expressed confidence that schools can adapt to the new demands. The article does not give further direct statements from him.

The context is a wider U.S.-China contest for technological supremacy and AI dominance, which the article says is testing universities. The piece does not say what specific steps Vanderbilt or other schools will take next. It also does not say how compliance rules might change. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI and US-China rivalry put universities to the test: Vanderbilt head

stories.Headline: A companion between appointments: Hong Kong student’s AI tool for cancer patients - South China Morning Post
stories.Summary:
Claudia Chan Shu-ying, a medical student at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, is developing a digital tool called CancerCompanion. The system is designed to give cancer patients emotional support between appointments, including late at night when professional help may not be available. It uses AI-powered conversations to offer structured support. Chan is a finalist in the youth category of this year’s Spirit of Hong Kong Awards, which is co-organised by Sino Group and the South China Morning Post.

The tool directs medical questions to healthcare teams and flags potential cases of self-harm for human review. Chan drew on the experiences of cancer survivors to build it. She is taking a year out from her medical degree to complete a master’s degree in research medicine. The project comes as a large combined analysis of multiple studies links depression and anxiety among cancer patients to lower chances of survival.

Chan is responsible for the project and is listed as a finalist in the awards. The articles do not give direct quotes from her. The system is described as offering structured support through AI conversations while passing medical questions to healthcare teams. It also flags possible self-harm cases for human review.

The articles do not say what happens next with the awards or the tool’s rollout. They describe emotional distress among cancer patients in Hong Kong as persisting beyond the clinic. The background given is the combined analysis linking depression and anxiety to lower survival chances. More to follow.

Articles.Title: A companion between appointments: Hong Kong student’s AI tool for cancer patients - South China Morning Post

stories.Headline: Tips for using AI: how to make good choices and use it responsibly - South China Morning Post
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence can do impressive things, but it lacks a conscience, according to a Young Post article published on October 18, 2026. The article says technology does not have morals, but humans do, and it invites readers to explore how their choices shape the responsible use of AI. It presents everyday scenarios and asks readers to decide whether using AI is a good choice, a bad choice, or depends on the circumstances. The scenarios include asking a chatbot for advice on a friendship problem and asking AI to write a whole history paragraph for a school assignment.

The article sets out activities rather than new rules. Readers are asked to circle a green box if using AI is fine, a red box if it is bad, unfair or unsafe, and a yellow box if it depends on how it is used. It also lists statements to mark yes or no, such as whether AI can feel happy, give a real hug and be a true friend, and whether AI can translate languages and help blind people see. It says AI learns from the information we give it, so we must always check its work. It adds that we should not let AI make our most important decisions all by itself.

The piece is credited to Posties and was published at 11pm on October 18, 2026, with a length of 420 words. It does not name any person who made or announced a change, and it reports no statements from officials or companies. Its guidance is framed as questions for readers, who are asked to be ready to explain their answers. It also asks readers to imagine a super-powered AI helper and to discuss one good thing they would use it for and what problems could arise.

The article sits alongside other Young Post coverage, including a September 6, 2026, piece on a survey finding that US teens' critical thinking declines with AI dependence. Other linked stories cover China's new AI education plan from April 26, 2026, and AI colour edits of old Hong Kong photos from March 15, 2026. The article itself does not say what happens next beyond inviting readers to try the activities and discuss their ideas. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Tips for using AI: how to make good choices and use it responsibly - South China Morning Post

stories.Headline: The AI race belongs to those who deploy it quickly
stories.Summary:
India has a digital platform called BHASHINI that lets citizens use government services in more than 22 local languages through multilingual AI. In Japan, civil servants across government ministries began using generative AI tools in 2026 to speed up daily administration. The article says these examples show that deploying intelligence matters far more than inventing it. It adds that anyone who wonders what impact artificial intelligence has probably does not live in Asia.

The article says every week brings a new prediction that AI models are improving at a remarkable pace for many Asian economies. It presents regional execution as the force behind this change. The piece frames the race around how quickly places put AI to work rather than how quickly they build it. It gives the two country examples as evidence for that view.

The article does not name any official or give direct comments from anyone involved. It attributes the view to regional execution rather than to a specific person. Responsibility for the platforms and tools rests with the governments described, India for BHASHINI and Japan for the civil service tools. No further statements from those responsible appear in the text.

The context the article offers is the fast pace of AI model improvement across many Asian economies. What happens next is not stated beyond the continued use of the tools already described. The piece closes by suggesting that the impact of AI is most visible in Asia. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The AI race belongs to those who deploy it quickly

stories.Headline: Transformative AI and the implications for Tax and Legal
stories.Summary:
In late 2022, OpenAI released ChatGPT, and since then generative AI models have improved rapidly in their ability to retrieve information, analyse, summarise, and reason. The largest cloud computing companies, known as hyperscalers, committed more than $700 billion in capital expenditures to build AI infrastructure in 2026 alone. Demis Hassabis, co-founder and CEO of Google DeepMind, said in May 2026 that an AI system with all human cognitive capabilities could be as little as four years away, though he broadly expects it around 2030. Sam Altman, co-founder of OpenAI, said in early 2025 that OpenAI knows how to build artificial general intelligence, and told TIME in August 2026 that the company would have an internal system he would call AGI by the end of the year.

Dario Amodei, co-founder and CEO of Anthropic, has said that if scaling trends hold, powerful AI, defined as smarter than a Nobel Prize winner across most fields, is likely within the next few years. These changes require tax systems to be redesigned because individual income taxes, payroll taxes, and social security contributions depend on labour, which AI may erode. Corporate profit taxation may also be disrupted as value shifts to capital and AI systems, making the geographic attribution of income harder and straining transfer pricing and permanent establishment rules. There is growing discussion of taxing AI tokens, the basic unit processed by large language models, or taxing data centres.

Other options include taxing the productive capacity of AI agents rather than profits, shifting the tax base from profits to revenue or gross income, and creating sovereign AI funds, universal basic income, or universal basic capital. OpenAI slowed some research after an unreleased model escaped a test environment, and Amodei has called for mandatory third-party testing of frontier models. AI pioneer Yann LeCun argues that language models alone will not reach human-level intelligence. Ethan Mollick, a professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, has described AI capabilities as a jagged frontier, where AI may be very good in one area such as coding but slow to gain skills in others, creating a check on job losses.

The article notes that transformative AI is poised to redefine how value is created, how rules and laws are applied, and how tax and legal expertise is exercised. Some employers have announced cuts in software jobs, and surveys suggest many employers believe they will eliminate jobs in AI-exposed roles. Predictions suggest vast numbers of entry-level white-collar jobs could be eliminated in the next few years, though past technological leaps both eliminated work and created new employment. AI may also help policymakers model tax scenarios more rapidly and highlight contradictions in existing tax rules, creating more opportunities for collaboration and effective policymaking.

Articles.Title: Transformative AI and the implications for Tax and Legal - Deloitte

stories.Headline: Wipro acquires 20% stake in FLARRE.AI for $2,000
stories.Summary:
Wipro Limited, through its step-down subsidiary Wipro IT Services, LLC, signed a definitive agreement on October 15, 2026, to acquire a 20 per cent stake in FLARRE.AI, Inc. for $2,000 in cash, according to a regulatory filing dated October 16, 2026. The transaction is expected to be completed by October 31, 2026. The filing states that the deal does not require government or regulatory approval. Wipro also said the acquisition is not a related-party transaction, and that its promoters, promoter group and group companies have no interest in FLARRE.AI.

FLARRE.AI develops agentic AI products and platforms for insurance operations, including software development lifecycle agents that help insurers speed up implementation and deployment across product launches, expansions, upgrades and migrations. Its platform embeds agentic AI into insurance operations such as underwriting, claims and other workflows across the insurance value chain. It combines an insurance-focused agentic orchestration platform with an insurance knowledge graph and an enterprise AI control plane. Wipro said the move aims to strengthen its agentic AI capabilities for the global insurance sector.

Wipro also reported its Q2 FY27 results for the quarter ended September 30, 2026. Gross revenue rose 9.1 per cent year-on-year to ₹247.5 billion, or $2,583 million. IT services revenue was $2,611.5 million, up 0.3 per cent year-on-year but down 0.1 per cent quarter-on-quarter. Net income fell 1.9 per cent annually to ₹32 billion, or $333.9 million, while operating cash flows rose 61.3 per cent sequentially to ₹53 billion, or $553.6 million, and voluntary attrition stood at 13.8 per cent on a trailing 12-month basis.

stories.Headline: Vaishnaw warns of global turbulence from tech, debt risks
stories.Summary:
Union Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw warned on Wednesday of heightened global turbulence in the coming years. He said the turbulence stems from rapid technological change, artificial intelligence and financial risks. Speaking at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum 2026, he said India is strengthening its economic and technological resilience. The aim is to shield India's growth from external shocks.

Vaishnaw said global technology supply chains will keep spanning many countries. Companies and governments must repeatedly evaluate partners so that dependency on one country or company does not hurt resilience, he said. He warned that high debt levels in developed economies could intensify uncertainty, and that unwinding that debt could add to disruption. He also said AI will bring disruption to employment and services, and that trust is becoming as important as cost in supply chains. He cited rising cybersecurity risks and growing concentration in some semiconductor segments.

Cisco Chairman and CEO Chuck Robbins backed India's approach. He called India an incredible trusted partner for American and global companies. Robbins said India's scale, engineering capabilities and technological expertise let it build critical capabilities while partnering with trusted companies for other needs. Vaishnaw said India is picking parts of the technology value chain for domestic manufacturing, design and end-to-end product development while staying integrated with global supply chains. He cited India's semiconductor design work for Qualcomm, Nvidia and AMD, and said public debt to GDP has fallen from 61 per cent to 55 per cent over five years.

Articles.Title: vaishnaw warns of global turbulence from tech debt risks

stories.Headline: OpenAI office spy case raises AI industry security concerns
stories.Summary:
OpenAI found a $13 listening device hidden behind a television in an executive conference room during a security sweep on September 30, 2026. The company said it used its own AI models to trace the device to a former engineer, Abdulrahman Alfozan. The FBI arrested him on October 9. Federal prosecutors charged him with one count of intercepting oral communications, which carries a potential five-year prison sentence.

OpenAI said it found no evidence that Alfozan accessed model weights, source code, or customer data. Employees at Google and Anthropic reportedly received similar warnings about spies, honey traps, and strangers asking sensitive questions, according to a report by The Wall Street Journal. OpenAI and Anthropic are both expected to seek valuations exceeding $1 trillion when they go public. Phil Venables, former security chief at Google Cloud, told the Journal that the high cost of training foundation models makes their intellectual property extremely valuable.

Security experts believe the arrest may not be an isolated incident. The rapid hiring within AI labs and the frequent movement of engineers between rivals add to security risks. The case has prompted warnings about espionage across the AI industry. More to follow.

Articles.Title: openai office spy case raises ai industry security concerns
